insider_note: Whenever the numerator's degree is at least the denominator's, always try adding and subtracting a constant to expose a cancelling factor before reaching for partial fractions.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Split using x²−1 = (x−1)(x+1)
steps.margin_note: First mark. x²/(1+x) = (x−1) + 1/(1+x) after the add-and-subtract-1 split — always check for a cancelling factor first.
steps.memory_tip: x² − 1 factors as (x−1)(x+1) — the (x+1) always cancels a (1+x) denominator.
steps.why: Adding and subtracting 1 in the numerator creates x²−1, which factors as (x−1)(x+1); the (x+1) factor cancels the denominator (1+x), leaving a plain polynomial plus one standard log term.
common_mistakes: Trying long division instead of the faster add-and-subtract-1 trick.
Forgetting that (x+1) and (1+x) are the same factor and failing to cancel.

steps.label: Integrate and apply the limits
steps.margin_note: Second mark. log1 = 0 always — the lower limit of the log term never contributes.
steps.memory_tip: 16/2 − 4 = 8 − 4 = 4 — check this arithmetic before combining with log5.
steps.why: The polynomial part integrates to x²/2 − x, evaluating to 4 at x=4 and 0 at x=0; the log part gives log5 at x=4 and log1=0 at x=0, so the two pieces add to 4+log5.
common_mistakes: Dropping the log1=0 term incorrectly, e.g. writing log(1+0) as 1 instead of 0.
An arithmetic slip in 16/2−4, e.g. getting 4 instead of the correct value.
